title: Plum's Perimeter Puzzle
markdown:
Oren made kites — sparkly dragons, giggling clouds, wobbly bumblebees that buzzed with joy if the wind was kind. His workshop smelled of glue and grass. His best friend was Plum, a fluffy hop-tastic rabbit whose ears could hear a dandelion puff from a mile away and whose nose wiggled like a tiny dancer when she was pleased.

Plum loved to zoom. Around her run like a furry blur. Past the juiciest carrots, which she sometimes remembered to eat. Under the shady bush, white tail a tiny flag. But the fence had danced a jig in a hurricane and forgotten how to stand. One moment left, the next right, a third moment nearly lying down as if it had finished being a fence. Plum felt a little dizzy and stopped mid-zoom to glare at a post, which did not help the post.

“This fence needs fixing,” Oren said one sunny morning, scratching until his hair stood like a startled dandelion. “A super-safe zoomable space. No wobbly surprises.” He rustled a big sheet of paper and a sparkly blue pencil. He drew a neat square. “Colourful edging all the way around the bottom. Stops sneaky weeds. A clear border for zoom-tracks. But — how much edging? The drawing is just a drawing. It doesn’t tell the real length.” He looked at the square, at Plum’s wide curious eyes, back at the square. His eyebrows did a confused little dance.

Plum twitched her nose — thinking. She nudged his hand with her velvety head. More zoom-space she understood. The how-much felt like catching a sunbeam in a teacup.

“Gran Maple,” Oren said, eyes lighting like a kite catching sun. “She measures gardens.” Off they went, sketch in hand, Plum hop-skip-hopping, ears flapping.

Maple’s cottage smelled of warm earth and blossoms. A kettle ticked in the kitchen and thought better of interrupting. She was humming, placing shiny blue tiles along the edge of her prize petunias — a neat line, little soldiers around pink and purple, each one kissing the next.

“A bit of a kerfuffle,” Oren called, out of breath. Plum sat on his boot to make the visit official.

Maple’s eyes crinkled. “What’s the excitement?”

He showed the square, paper still warm from being clutched. “Edging around Plum’s new run. I tried to measure the drawing with my thumb. Too small for the real size. The thumb lied.”

She chuckled, dry leaves on a path, and held out a tile still cool from the stack. “I lay them one after another. This line follows the flower bed. Same size each, so when I count, I know how long this edge is — how much space the roots may stretch.” She ran a finger along the row, tapping every fifth tile so the number would stay honest. “All the way around would mean the same job on every side. Not a guess. A walk with counting in it.”

Oren looked from drawing to tiles to Plum, who gave a bunny-wiggle. PING. “We can do that at home.”

They thanked her and hurried back. In the workshop, a pile of smooth grey stones, each about a thumb. Perfect. Plum nudged them into line, surprisingly good at it.

Oren set one. “One bit of the edge.” Another. Clink. “Two.” End to end along the first side of the marked square, stones touching like Maple’s tiles. “One through eight.” Plum inspected the line with her nose and pushed the fifth stone a whisker to the left until it behaved.

The next side shared a corner stone already counted, so seven new ones: nine through fifteen. Whiskers twitching. Third side, another shared corner: sixteen through twenty-two. A bee landed on twenty and left, unimpressed. Fourth side, two corners already placed: twenty-three through twenty-eight. The last stone clicked like a puzzle piece.

He walked the ring again, pointing, so the corners would not be paid twice. Eight on the first walk, then only the new stones after that. Twenty-eight. “That’s how much edging. All the way around.” Plum sat in the exact middle and turned once, as if testing whether the square felt like a square from inside.

The total distance around the outside had a name: perimeter. All the sides added up — a path that went around. Knowing it meant knowing the ribbon.

At the craft shop he bought bright red, zig-zag yellow, stripey blue, grassy green, measured in stone-lengths to twenty-eight. Soon Plum had a sturdy new run. She zoomed and zipped, leaving tiny tracks along the cheerful edging, secure enough to hop her heart out.

She nudged his hand, wet-nose thanks. Oren felt light as a kite and did not wonder about kite-tails or the edge of his bed. He wrote 28 on the workshop wall beside the square sketch, in numbers large enough to see from the carrots, so the next fence would not start as a guess. Plum flicked her tail and took the perimeter at full zoom, which was, after all, the point of measuring it.
